o: Sorted nums consists of n lower values and their n partners shifted by 2k. The smallest element must belong to lower, so its partner nums[0] + 2k exists somewhere in nums — each positive even difference (nums[j] - nums[0]) / 2 is a candidate k. For each candidate, greedily pair every unconsumed smallest remaining value x with x + 2k; if all 2n values pair up, the paired lowers plus k recover arr. With n <= 1000 there are at most 2n candidates and each check is O(n), well within limits. Example 1: nums[0]=2, candidate from 6 gives k=2, pairing succeeds producing [3,7,11].
k: After sorting, nums[0] is always a lower element, so 2k = nums[j] - nums[0] for some j.
Greedy smallest-first pairing with a multiset correctly validates a candidate k.
At least one candidate is guaranteed to succeed.

a.n: Approach 1: Enumerate k Candidates + Greedy Pairing
a.i: Try every achievable 2k from the minimum element, validate by consuming values from a counter smallest-first, and return the first complete pairing.
s: Sort nums; for each j with (nums[j]-nums[0]) positive and even, set k = difference / 2.
Copy a frequency counter of nums; scan values ascending: for each x still available, require x+2k available; consume both and record x+k.
If the scan consumes everything, return the recorded arr; otherwise try the next candidate.
a.t: O(n^2) — up to 2n candidates, each validated in O(n) with hash lookups
a.sp: O(n) for the counter and answer

w: Key correctness point: processing values in sorted order guarantees the smaller partner of each pair is met first, so greedy consumption is safe. Pitfalls: k must be strictly positive (reject d = 0), and 2k must be even. Example 2 shows why k = 0 is invalid. Follow-up: prove at least one candidate always succeeds given the problem guarantee.
